editor_spans.body: Read the Ukraine stories in date order and a domestic motive shows through the 'rock-solid' language. On 9 October the government responded to a US-Russia agreement, and half of what it said was about energy prices and the cost of living. On 12 October the Prime Minister described an energy ceasefire as 'the quickest way' to get diesel back onto world markets, and he welcomed President Trump's reciprocal version. By 14 October Downing Street was listing Russia's attacks on energy infrastructure 'since President Trump called for an energy ceasefire'. London's position therefore rests on a US initiative that Moscow is ignoring, and on a fuel-price problem at home that London does not control.

The numbers deserve a closer look than the word 'accelerate' gets. Of the £45 million missile package, £10 million is being brought forward. The underlying £1.6 billion for more than 5,000 LMMs is spread over four years. The new sanctions, military and fiscal packages exist so far only as an instruction to ministers to draw them up. There is also a tension inside the policy: the UK is asking partners to join a maritime services ban on Russian LNG while it frets about energy prices. That is a real cost, and it gets talked about only as a sacrifice for others to share.

The Great British Railways headquarters is better read as regional policy than as railway reform. The building holds up to 450 staff, it won't be finished until spring 2029, and it sits next to Alstom's Derby site, which already has the £1 billion northern train order. The apprenticeship figures are small next to the problem the announcement itself names. Up to 600 places over four years, for the whole national railway, is a slow answer to a workforce where fewer than 7% are under 25. The fares freeze and extra seats are the claims passengers will actually judge it on. Where the head office goes will matter far less to them.

The 'offer' to Holyrood is a challenge presented as cooperation. A Prime Minister who used to be a metro mayor, and who now runs No10 North, is calling the Scottish Government one of Europe's most centralised devolved administrations. He also proposes to reach Scotland's regions through the Scotland Office. That gives Westminster a way to build relationships with Scottish councils and cities that go round the First Minister. The same week, he told the Commons he wants a 'serious dialogue' on long-term options for the UK's relationship with the EU. Both moves reopen questions about where power sits, and the Brussels summit on 20 November will show whether he can deliver on the first of them.
